content_voiceover: This slide covers two board-relevant myeloma supportive care topics: bone disease management and infection prophylaxis. For skeletal-related events, NCCN guidelines say every myeloma patient getting active treatment should receive a bone-targeted agent, either a bisphosphonate or denosumab, though local reimbursement may restrict coverage to those with proven lytic disease. Before starting, get a dental exam and clear any needed dental work first, because these drugs carry a jaw osteonecrosis risk; avoid procedures like extractions or implants for ninety days around dosing. Zoledronic acid is four milligrams IV over at least fifteen minutes, dose-adjusted for renal function and held if creatinine clearance is under thirty; denosumab is one hundred twenty milligrams subcutaneous every four weeks and is the preferred option in renal impairment since it isn't renally cleared. Bisphosphonate therapy is typically capped around two years, though continuation is a shared decision; denosumab is generally continued longer, sometimes spaced to every six months, and stopping it requires a bisphosphonate dose afterward to prevent rebound osteoporosis. Meanwhile, all patients should be screened for hepatitis B and C before first-line therapy. Anyone on a proteasome inhibitor, an anti-CD38 or anti-SLAMF7 antibody, a bispecific, CAR-T, or a recent autologous transplant needs herpes zoster and HSV prophylaxis with valacyclovir, acyclovir, or famcyclovir, especially if seropositive. Antifungal prophylaxis with fluconazole or an echinocandin is considered for severe mucositis or neutropenia under five hundred for more than a week post-transplant.
keypoints: Bone-targeted therapy: bisphosphonate or denosumab for all active-treatment myeloma patients
Dental exam before starting; avoid dental procedures 90 days around dosing (osteonecrosis risk)
Denosumab preferred if CrCl under 30; stopping it needs a bisphosphonate dose to prevent rebound osteoporosis
Screen hepatitis B and C before first-line therapy
Antiviral prophylaxis with PI, CD38/SLAMF7 antibody, CAR-T, or after autologous transplant
keypoint_voiceover: Remember three exam pearls. First, all myeloma patients on active treatment get a bone-targeted agent, dental clearance first, and a ninety-day dental procedure blackout around dosing. Second, denosumab is preferred when renal function is poor, and stopping it needs a bisphosphonate dose to prevent rebound osteoporosis. Third, screen hepatitis B and C up front, and give herpes prophylaxis with proteasome inhibitors, CD38 antibodies, bispecifics, CAR-T, or after autologous transplant.
